article_content: Claudio Ranieri has reportedly received a €4 million severance package from AS Monaco following his unexpected dismissal last May. Despite guiding the team to promotion in his first season (2012-13) and securing a second-place Champions League qualification finish in 2013-14, the 62-year-old Italian manager was relieved of his duties at season's end. Monaco's vice-president Vasim Vasilyev described the decision as 'difficult' during a press conference, stating: 'While the results were positive, we felt the project required fresh momentum.' Ranieri's departure came after he successfully returned the club to Ligue 1 prominence but fell short of challenging Paris Saint-Germain's domestic dominance. The managerial reins have now passed to Leonardo Jardim, formerly of Sporting Lisbon. He inherits a squad featuring prominent names including Colombian striker Radamel Falcao, Bulgarian forward Dimitar Berbatov, and World Cup standout James Rodriguez. Reports suggest Ranieri may be considering an international management role with Greece's national team.

article_content: Newly revealed photographs from the archive of cinema photographer Arthur Lemon showcase Lauren Bacall's devoted family life during Humphrey Bogart's 1951 filming of 'The African Queen' in the Belgian Congo (modern-day Democratic Republic of the Congo). The collection, rediscovered by Lemon's son Chris following Bacall's recent passing at 89, provides intimate glimpses of Hollywood legends working in challenging jungle conditions. Bogart and co-star Katherine Hepburn filmed in the then-Belgian Congo, with Bacall traveling to support her husband during the production. Lemon's images capture both professional collaboration and personal bonds, including Bacall's extended stay with their young son. 'Dad returned with incredible stories,' Chris recalled, 'including close wildlife encounters and makeshift celebrations amidst the risks.' Security teams with rifles protected cast and crew from local wildlife threats. The photographs resurfaced as the world mourned Bacall's death, highlighting her enduring connection to Bogart despite her own illustrious career. Though best remembered for 1940s classics like 'To Have and Have Not' and her iconic whistle line, Bacall's later years saw her fight for recognition beyond being 'Bogie's widow,' eventually earning an honorary Oscar in 2009 after decades of acclaimed stage and screen work.
